receipt.public_excerpt: The FT said the company ⁠raised $122 billion in March at an $852 billion valuation but is on track ​to exhaust that cash by 2028.

evidence_items.explanation: OpenAI expects $278B of negative free cash flow from 2026 to 2030 and expects to run out of its raised cash by 2028. It cannot fund its compute from operations, but it is currently funded by investors.

receipt.public_excerpt: about 80% of the $518 billion it's committed must be paid regardless of how much computing power the company actually uses.

evidence_items.explanation: Anthropic's mostly non-cancellable $518B of compute commitments compare with $20.28B in cash at the end of 2025, as the same article reports. So the commitments depend on future revenue and financing.

receipt.public_excerpt: They are multi-year obligations against revenue that has been growing quickly but has not yet reached the scale the contracts assume.

evidence_items.explanation: This supports the view that current revenue does not cover the contracts. The same article calls the arithmetic 'defensible' given that Anthropic's run rate had passed $30bn.

receipt.public_excerpt: Anthropic has told ⁠shareholders that its adjusted ‌operating income will be positive for a second ​straight quarter

evidence_items.explanation: Anthropic was operating profitably on an adjusted basis, which weakens a flat claim that it cannot afford compute. It does not show it can cover hundreds of billions in commitments.

unresolved_gaps: Whether OpenAI and Anthropic can meet their compute payments depends on future revenue and fundraising that had not happened by the evaluation date.
No missed or renegotiated compute payment by either company was found.
The speaker gave no standard for 'afford'. The outcome turns on whether relying on outside financing counts as being unable to afford.
